prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "NETFLIX INC" (ticker NFLX), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "NFLX", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Netflix, Inc.
markets: Video podcasts and consumer products / Netflix House experiences

mission.source: Netflix Q1 2026 shareholder letter ("Our mission remains ambitious and unchanged: to entertain the world."); the Netflix Culture Memo opens "At Netflix, we aspire to entertain the world, thrilling audiences everywhere."
mission.plain: Make shows, films and games that people everywhere love to watch and play.

about.plain: Netflix is an app where you pay a monthly fee to watch TV shows and movies whenever you want. It makes many of its own shows, like Stranger Things, Squid Game and KPop Demon Hunters, and buys others from studios. It works on TVs, phones and computers in almost every country. It is now also adding live sports and events, games and video podcasts.
about.customers: Hundreds of millions of households around the world that pay a monthly subscription, plus advertisers who pay to show ads on the cheaper plan.
about.everyday: When someone says they spent the weekend 'binge-watching' a series, there is a good chance they were watching it on Netflix.

money.plain: monthly plans to watch shows and movies
ads shown on the cheaper ad plan (about $1.5B in 2025, guided to roughly $3B in 2026)
live boxing, NFL Christmas games, WWE Raw, baseball
mobile games, TV party games and a kids' game app

result.summary: Yes. Netflix is the largest paid streaming service in the world, and that scale gives it a strong advantage: its 2025 revenue of $45.2B lets it spend about $17B a year on content while still earning a 29.5% operating margin, which rivals losing money on streaming cannot match. Its brand, recommendation engine, global reach of local-language hits and very low churn reinforce one another, though YouTube's free video and the newly merged Paramount-Warner Bros. (Skydance) are serious rivals for viewing time.

pricingPower.evidence: Netflix raised US prices again in March 2026 (Standard with ads $7.99 to $8.99, Standard $17.99 to $19.99, Premium $24.99 to $26.99) after earlier rises in January 2025, and said in its Q2 2026 letter that the results of recent price changes were consistent with prior changes and expectations; revenue still grew 13.4% year on year to $12.56B in Q2 2026.

moats.evidence: Netflix is a household name in over 190 countries and its own franchises (Stranger Things, Squid Game, Wednesday, Bridgerton, KPop Demon Hunters) are owned intellectual property it can extend into games, live experiences and merchandise.
Members can cancel any month at no cost; personalised profiles, watch history and household habits add only mild friction.

More members fund more content, which attracts more members, and viewing data across a global base improves recommendations and commissioning; cultural 'watercooler' hits also spread by word of mouth, though this is an indirect scale effect rather than a true user-to-user network.

With $45.2B of 2025 revenue, Netflix spreads its ~$17.1B content spend (2025 additions to content assets) over more paying households than any rival, earning a 29.5% operating margin while most legacy media streaming units have only recently reached break-even.
Global streaming supports several large players (YouTube, Amazon, Disney, Skydance), so the market is not naturally limited to one provider.

Netflix never had a cable or theatrical business to protect, so it could go all-in on direct-to-consumer streaming while incumbents hesitated; that edge has faded as rivals moved to streaming, but it still avoids the costs of linear TV networks.

Two decades of personalisation algorithms, its Open Connect content-delivery network and a proven local-production machine in 50+ countries (Korea, Spain, India, Mexico) are hard to replicate quickly.

Exclusive rights to its growing original library, multi-year deals with top creators (e.g. Shonda Rhimes, the Duffer Brothers previously) and exclusive live rights such as WWE Raw and NFL Christmas Day games, but talent and sports rights can be outbid.

customers.evidence: Netflix has historically reported the lowest churn among major US streaming services in third-party trackers such as Antenna, and it kept growing revenue (16% in 2025, 13.4% in Q2 2026) through repeated price increases; it stopped reporting member counts in 2025, after passing 300 million paid memberships.

talent.evidence: Its famous Culture Memo, policy of paying top-of-market salaries and 'freedom and responsibility' culture attract strong engineers and creatives; about 16,000 full-time employees at end-2025, though the 'keeper test' culture is seen by some as harsh.

product.evidence: Netflix's series and films regularly win Emmys and Oscars, its app runs on almost every TV, phone and console, and Nielsen's Gauge shows it with 7.9% of all US TV viewing in June 2026, the largest share of any subscription streaming service (behind only free YouTube).

competitors.name: Alphabet (YouTube)
competitors.note: YouTube is the biggest source of TV-screen viewing in the US (13.5% share in June 2026) and competes for viewing time, creators and ad dollars.

competitors.name: The Walt Disney Company (Disney+, Hulu, ESPN)
competitors.note: Direct subscription streaming rival with Disney+, Hulu and ESPN streaming; competes for subscribers, talent and content.

competitors.name: Skydance (Paramount + Warner Bros. Discovery: Paramount+, HBO Max)
competitors.note: Merged in October 2026 after outbidding Netflix for Warner Bros.; owns HBO, Warner Bros. and Paramount studios and over 200 million streaming subscriptions.

competitors.name: Amazon (Prime Video)
competitors.note: Prime Video bundled with Prime, with ads by default, MGM studio library, NBA and NFL Thursday Night Football rights.

competitors.name: Comcast (Peacock, NBCUniversal)
competitors.note: Peacock streaming, Universal films and NBC sports compete for subscribers, content and sports rights.

competitors.name: Apple (Apple TV)
competitors.note: Apple TV subscription service with premium originals and MLS/F1 rights; competes for talent and prestige content.

competitors.name: ByteDance (TikTok)
competitors.note: Short-form video competes for leisure screen time, especially among younger viewers.

competitors.name: Roku
competitors.note: The Roku Channel free ad-supported streaming and its TV platform compete for viewing and CTV ad budgets; also a key distribution partner.

competitors.name: Fox Corporation (Tubi)
competitors.note: Tubi free ad-supported streaming and Fox One compete for viewing time and ad dollars.

competitors.name: Tencent (Tencent Video)
competitors.note: Leading Chinese streaming service; Netflix does not operate in mainland China, so overlap is mainly for Asian content and talent.

competitors.name: iQIYI
competitors.note: Chinese streaming platform expanding in Southeast Asia through iQIYI International.

competitors.name: Spotify
competitors.note: Competes in video podcasts, a format Netflix entered in 2026, and for subscription wallet share.

competitors.name: Sony Group (Sony Pictures, PlayStation)
competitors.note: Films and video games compete for entertainment time, though Sony is also a major content licensor to Netflix.

estimates.name: Paramount Skydance (before Warner Bros. Discovery merger)
Warner Bros. Discovery (acquired by Skydance Oct 2026)

marketShare.market: Share of total US TV viewing time (Nielsen The Gauge; June 2026 vs May 2021)

threats: YouTube's free, creator-made video keeps taking a larger share of TV viewing (13.5% vs Netflix's 7.9% in June 2026) and is winning younger audiences.

Skydance, formed in October 2026 from Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery after it outbid Netflix for Warner Bros., combines HBO, Warner Bros. and Paramount libraries into a stronger rival and may pull licensed content back.
Slowing growth after the password-sharing boost faded: Q3 2026 revenue guidance of 11.7% growth disappointed and the shares fell more than 40% from their mid-2025 high.
Rising costs of sports and live rights and of top talent could squeeze margins as Netflix pushes into live events.
Short-form video (TikTok, Instagram Reels) and AI-generated video competing for leisure time.
Price-increase fatigue and household budget pressure could raise churn, especially in emerging markets.
Reduced disclosure (no more member counts, engagement report moving to annual in 2027) may make it harder for investors to judge momentum.

ceo.name: Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters (co-CEOs)
ceo.background: Sarandos: former video-store clerk and film distributor, joined Netflix in 2000 as content chief, co-CEO since 2020; Peters: physics and astronomy graduate (Yale), joined in 2008, ran product and was COO before becoming co-CEO in January 2023.

c1.evidence: Netflix is the global leader in paid streaming ($45.2B 2025 revenue, over 300 million paid memberships when last reported) but streaming is no longer an emerging industry and its growth has slowed to about 12-14% in 2026.

c2.evidence: Customers choose it for the deepest library of hit originals across languages and a best-in-class app, funded by a ~$17B yearly content budget that rivals cannot match profitably, which makes the advantage durable though not unassailable.

c3.evidence: Netflix is the default name for streaming ('Netflix and chill', 'binge-watch'), and the prompt itself cites it as an example of a field's default leader.

c4.evidence: Its mission 'to entertain the world' is repeated in every shareholder letter and the Culture Memo, but it is an entertainment goal rather than a deeply purpose-driven one, and management is heavily focused on margins and buybacks ($4.7B in Q2 2026).

c6.evidence: “binge-watching, entertaining, original shows, getting pricier” — the impression is mostly positive, tempered by complaints about repeated price rises and cancelled series.

c7.evidence: Netflix estimates it has captured only a small share of global TV viewing and entertainment spend, streaming reached 48.5% of US TV viewing in June 2026, and connected-TV advertising is a growing secular market.

c8.evidence: It is expanding into advertising (about $3B expected in 2026, roughly double 2025), live sports and events, games, video podcasts and Netflix House venues.

m1.evidence: Sarandos and Peters have a clear plan (ads, live, games, AI tools via the InterPositive acquisition), but the original vision of streaming belonged to founder Reed Hastings.

m2.evidence: Neither co-CEO is a founder, but both are long-tenured (Sarandos since 2000, Peters since 2008) and run the company with a long-term, culture-first mindset inherited from Hastings.

m4.evidence: Netflix pays top-of-market salaries and grants wide freedom, but its 'keeper test' culture prioritises performance over employee security.

m5.evidence: The Netflix Culture Memo (freedom and responsibility, candour, the keeper test) is one of the most famous corporate cultures and has driven innovations from streaming to the ad tier and live events, though it was mainly built by Reed Hastings.

m6.evidence: Greg Peters is a technologist who led product and technology, while Ted Sarandos is a content executive with no engineering background.

m7.evidence: Both co-CEOs have good reputations and support causes such as Sarandos's philanthropy for education and film preservation, but there is no clear evidence their stewardship is aimed at something bigger than entertainment and profit.

m7b.evidence: No verified commencement speech at Stanford, Harvard or MIT by Ted Sarandos or Greg Peters was found.

m8b.evidence: Sarandos is a well-known Hollywood figure, but neither co-CEO has a famous, larger-than-life public persona like Elon Musk or Alex Karp.

m9.evidence: Since the co-CEO structure began in 2023, revenue rose from $33.7B (2023) to $45.2B (2025) and operating margin from 20.6% to 29.5%, with the ad tier and paid-sharing rollouts executed successfully.

m10.evidence: Netflix is known for paying top-of-market salaries and spending heavily on content rather than for frugality, although its culture discourages bureaucracy and wasteful processes.

c10.evidence: Netflix entertains hundreds of millions of households in over 190 countries and brings local-language stories (e.g. Squid Game from Korea, Money Heist from Spain) to global audiences.

p2.evidence: Streaming high-quality video reliably to hundreds of millions of devices and producing hits in dozens of languages is hard, but entertainment is less essential to the world than medicine, energy or computing.

f1.evidence: Revenue grew every year from FY2020 to FY2025: $25.0B, $29.7B, $31.6B, $33.7B, $39.0B, $45.2B.

f2.evidence: Gross margin rose from 41.6% in 2021 to 48.5% in 2025 and operating margin from 20.9% to 29.5%, with only a dip in 2022.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 total debt was $14.3B against $9.1B of cash and short-term investments, 2025 free cash flow of $9.5B and stockholders' equity of $30.2B, so debt is about 1.5 years of free cash flow.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $6.19B (2021) to $13.33B (2025) and operating cash flow from $0.39B to $10.15B, with a dip only in 2022 for operating income.

v1.evidence: Netflix has the largest share of US TV viewing of any subscription service (7.9% in June 2026) and the broadest slate of hits, but whether it is 'best' depends on taste, and free YouTube plus HBO Max and Disney+ offer strong alternatives.

v2.evidence: Netflix's culture and pay make it a coveted employer in tech and Hollywood, but no verified top-10 placement in recent Glassdoor or Fortune best-places-to-work rankings was found, and its high-performance culture is polarising.

c5.evidence: If Netflix disappeared, hundreds of millions of families would miss their favourite shows and creators in many countries would lose a global outlet, though rival streamers would fill much of the gap.
